extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and human-rights observers interested in Nepali media law and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A country-level survey of legal frameworks, institutions, and practices that enable or restrict expression in Nepal across media, internet, film, political and religious domains. Summarizes constitutional provisions, government directives, institutional actors, and notable incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantee of freedom of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution of Nepal guarantees the fundamental rights of citizens, including the freedom of expression; the right includes freedom of opinion and thought no matter what the source is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes tension across constitutional versions: the 1990 constitution (Article 115) explicitly outlawed censorship, while later reforms (2004, 2009, 2015) contain restrictions described as obscure and open to misinterpretation compared to 1990. Use of emergency clauses (e.g., Clause 1 of Article 115 in 2001–2002) shows that constitutionally-guaranteed rights can be suspended in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: No direct censorship of media (constitutional ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The media, under the Constitution, should not be subject to direct censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International observers urged a progressive media policy aligned with the constitution; however, draft policies and later directives have conflicted with this principle. Evaluation of media systems should check whether formal policies prohibit direct censorship and whether implementation matches the legal ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online Media Directives 2015 (authority to censor/shut down online media)
rubrics_metrics.description: The government approved the Online Media Directives 2015, which provides for censorship or shut-down of online media based on their contents, a measure that critics say denies the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the Directives as a regulatory standard that can override constitutional practice in implementation. Examples: takedowns and shutdowns cited in the article. When assessing online media freedom, verify whether such directives exist, their scope, and whether they include notice, appeal, or judicial oversight mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom vs. emergency suspension (Article 115, 1990)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 115 of the 1990 Constitution outlawed any form of censorship and strongly guaranteed a free press; yet emergency provisions were invoked in 2001–2002 to suspend these freedoms (king's interventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should include whether emergency or public-order clauses permit suspension of press freedoms, and historical patterns of invoking those clauses. Examples: arrests, beatings, detentions and killings of journalists in 2001–2002; subsequent protests in 2006 that restored some press freedoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes of conduct (Nepal Press Council and FNJ) and enforcement gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nepal Press Council and the Federation of Nepali Journalists (FNJ) have a code of conduct, but it lacks effective systems and mechanisms and needs more support from media stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating press self-regulation assess both the presence of codes and the strength of enforcement mechanisms, resources, and stakeholder support. A code without enforcement does not prevent censorship or protect journalists in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: State control of internet infrastructure as a censorship lever
rubrics_metrics.description: The government controls the Internet in Nepal and has cut international internet connections (e.g., during martial law declared by the King in 2005).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infrastructure-level control (control of gateways, ISPs) is a substantive censorship mechanism; analyses should examine whether authorities can and do sever connectivity, block services, or use infrastructure to restrict access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-censorship driven by intimidation and threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-censorship can be forced on internet content by intimidation, as happened when the satirical folk song 'Lutna Sake Lut' was taken down by the author amid threats to his person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond formal laws, social and extra-legal pressures (threats, violence) produce self-censorship. Evaluate safety environment for creators, incidence of threats, and examples of content removals due to fear rather than formal orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social-media/platform registration and local-representative requirements (2023 rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities required platforms to register and appoint local representatives to monitor content and abide by 2023 rules; failure to comply led to bans (e.g., announcement of bans on multiple platforms; TikTok was banned in 2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory obligations on platforms (registration, local contact points, content-removal duties) are criteria for assessing internet freedom and the risk of platform-level blocking. Note enforcement outcomes: bans, public unrest, resignations, and committee formation to probe incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film Censor Board controls sex, violence, and politics in film
rubrics_metrics.description: The Film Censor Board (established 1951) controls sex, violence, and politics in film, commands cuts of scenes harmful to society and the state, and can discredit certification or prohibit whole films deemed inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship of visual media often targets sexual content, violence, and political themes; typical practices include chunked removals of sexual scenes and certification denial. Assess whether certification decisions are transparent, criteria-based, and whether cuts degrade cinematic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political censorship and direct suppression of political expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Any forms of publications that contain political thoughts or opinions are censored by the government; police suppress journalists and force self-censorship when criticism of politicians or politics appears (e.g., newspapers burned, journalists arrested over political cartoons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging political expression protections, examine incidents of direct suppression (seizure, arrests, violence), the legality cited for actions, and whether journalists face criminal sanctions or extralegal reprisals for political content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious censorship and prohibitions on conversion/defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-2006 constitutions prohibited acts leading to conversions; the government controls religious expression or defamation, especially when content publicly dissents from Hinduism or offends Hindu sentiments (examples: Komal Oli's song banned from Nepal Television; police shut down an art gallery displaying depictions of Hindu gods in unconventional ways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should consider legal prohibitions on conversion, blasphemy/defamation provisions, and patterns of enforcement against artistic or religious dissent. Note that religious-sentiment protections may be applied to restrict artistic expression and media content.
